title: King Canute and the Tide
text:
Cnut, often called Canute, was a Danish prince who conquered England in 1016 and went on to rule Denmark and Norway too. He was one of the most powerful kings in Europe.

About a hundred years after his death the English chronicler Henry of Huntingdon told a story about him. At the height of his power, Cnut had his chair placed on the shore as the tide was rising. He said to the sea that it was subject to him, and that the land on which he sat was his, and he commanded the water not to rise onto his land or wet his clothes or limbs.

The tide came in as usual and soaked his feet and legs. The king jumped back and said, in Henry's account, that everyone should know how empty and worthless is the power of kings, for no one deserves the name of king except the one whom heaven, earth and sea obey by eternal laws.

Henry adds that Cnut never wore his golden crown again, but placed it on a crucifix. The story is often remembered backwards, as a tale of royal arrogance. In the original, the king staged it to teach humility.
lesson: Know the limits of your power and do not let flattery hide them from you. Sometimes it helps to show others those limits plainly.
location: England (shore not named; later tradition suggests Southampton or Bosham)
source: Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum, Book 6
caveat: The story is first recorded about a century after Cnut's death and may be a moral tale rather than a real event.
